lesson.subject: data-ai
lesson.title: Search Engines: How Computers Find Answers
lesson.summary: See how crawlers and an index power a search engine, choose good keywords, understand ranking and adverts, and check what you find.
learning_objectives: Explain how a crawler and an index help a search engine find pages
Understand ranking and adverts, and check sources safely

standards.text: Understand computer networks including the internet; use search technologies effectively, appreciate how results are selected and ranked, and be discerning in evaluating digital content
Use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; identify a range of ways to report concerns

success_criteria: I can say what a crawler and an index do
I can choose clear keywords and fix a search
I know that top results and adverts are not proof, and I check sources
lesson.real_life: Searching for facts about mountains, rivers or a school project, then checking more than one trusted source.

warm_up.explanation: The internet is a network of networks.

options.text: A network that joins computers all over the world

warm_up.hint: You visit it in a browser.
warm_up.explanation: A website is a group of linked pages.

blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how does a search engine find answers?
blocks.say: Today we find out how a search engine finds answers. How can it search so quickly?

blocks.alt: A brass magnifying glass with a red handle lying on a polished wooden table beside an antique lamp base
blocks.caption: A magnifying glass helps us find small things. A search engine helps us find web pages.
blocks.credit: Photo by Alexandr Popadin on Unsplash
blocks.say: Zara wants to know how high the mountain K2 is. A magnifying glass helps us find small things.

blocks.markdown: The web is pages joined by **links**.
blocks.say: The web is millions of pages joined together. A page can have links that open other pages.

blocks.markdown: A **crawler** is a program that visits pages by following links.
blocks.say: A search engine uses a program called a crawler. It visits a page, then follows every link on it.

scenes.caption: Start.
scenes.say: The crawler starts on one page. It spots three links.

scenes.caption: Follow.
scenes.say: It follows each link to a new page. Then it follows the links on those pages.

scenes.caption: Explore.
scenes.say: Page by page, the crawler explores more and more of the web.

question.prompt: A program visits a page, then follows its links to find more pages. What kind of program is it?
question.hint: It crawls from page to page.
question.explanation: A crawler follows links to find pages.

blocks.markdown: An **index** is a giant list of the words and pages the crawler found.
blocks.say: The crawler saves what it finds in a giant list. That list is called the index.

blocks.markdown: An index helps us find things fast.
blocks.say: A book has an index at the back too. It helps you find a topic without reading every page.

scenes.caption: Type.
scenes.say: Zara types K2 height into the search box.

scenes.caption: Look up.
scenes.say: The search engine does not visit the whole web again. It looks in its index.

scenes.caption: Results.
scenes.say: It lists pages that match her words. This takes a fraction of a second.

question.prompt: Where does a search engine look when you press search?
question.explanation: It looks in the index its crawler built.

options.text: In its index of saved pages

blocks.title: Zara searches for K2
blocks.transcript: Zara wonders how high the mountain K2 is. She opens a search engine. She types the important words only: K2 height metres. Long before, a crawler followed links from page to page and filled an index. The search engine looks in its index. A ranked list of results appears. The first result says Ad. A company paid for it, so Zara skips it. She opens a mountain survey page. It names the writer and the date. A second trusted page gives the same height. The sources agree. She used safe search and never typed her address. She tells her teacher the answer.
blocks.caption: Zara searches for how high K2 is and checks her sources.

blocks.markdown: **Keywords** are the important words you type to search.
blocks.say: Zara wants K2's height. She picks the important words. These are called keywords.

scenes.caption: Vague.
scenes.say: Zara tries a search: tell me about that big thing. It is too vague.

scenes.caption: Clear.
scenes.say: Now she types K2 height metres. Every word is useful.

scenes.caption: Better.
scenes.say: Clear keywords help the search engine find the pages you really want.

blocks.title: Sort the searches
blocks.goal: Move the 6 searches into Clear keywords or Too vague.

question.prompt: Which search would best find how long the River Indus is?

blocks.say: If the results are wrong, change your words. Check your spelling. Add a word to be clearer.

scenes.caption: Mixed.
scenes.say: Zara searches for jaguar and sees cars and animals.

scenes.caption: Add a word.
scenes.say: She adds one word: jaguar animal. Now she sees only animals.

scenes.caption: Try again.
scenes.say: Changing a search is not a failure. It is how good searchers work.

blocks.markdown: **Ranking** is the order of results, with the likeliest matches first.
blocks.say: A search can find thousands of pages. The search engine puts them in an order. That order is a ranking.

blocks.alt: A red, yellow and blue winners podium numbered 1, 2 and 3 on grass beside a running track
blocks.caption: A podium ranks winners. A search engine ranks pages.
blocks.say: At a race, a podium shows who came first, second and third. Search results are ranked in a similar way.

scenes.caption: Match.
scenes.say: The engine checks if the page matches the words Zara typed.

scenes.caption: Links.
scenes.say: It checks if many other pages link to it. Links can show a page is useful.

scenes.caption: Many clues.
scenes.say: It also looks at how new the page is. Many clues together decide the ranking.

question.prompt: Which is one clue a search engine can use to rank a page?
question.explanation: Links from other pages can be a ranking clue.

options.text: The size of the writer's shoes
How many other pages link to it

blocks.markdown: An **advert** is paid for. It is not chosen as the best answer.
blocks.say: Some results are adverts. A company pays for them to appear. They should be labelled Ad or Sponsored.

blocks.markdown: Page owners can try to influence the ranking. Play the memory game.
blocks.say: Companies can also improve their own pages so they are easier to find. First a memory game.

blocks.markdown: Check the **source**: who made the page?
blocks.say: Zara finds two pages about K2. They give slightly different heights. She needs to decide which to trust.

blocks.markdown: Look at who made the page.
blocks.say: First, she checks who wrote it. A museum or a mountain survey is easier to trust than a stranger.
Second, she checks the date. Third, she compares a second source. Good facts usually agree.

scenes.caption: Page one.
scenes.say: Page one is from a mountain survey. It names the writer and the date.

scenes.caption: Page two.
scenes.say: Page two has no writer and lots of flashing adverts.

scenes.caption: Agree.
scenes.say: A third trusted page agrees with page one. Zara trusts that answer.

blocks.markdown: Use **safe search**, and tell a grown-up if something upsets you.
blocks.say: Safe search hides many unsuitable results. It does not check facts, so we still check sources.

blocks.markdown: Keep private things private when you search.
blocks.say: Zara never types her address or school into a search box. Private things stay private.

scenes.caption: Turn on.
scenes.say: Zara turns on safe search before she starts.

scenes.caption: Close and tell.
scenes.say: A strange page appears. She closes it and tells her teacher.

scenes.caption: Private.
scenes.say: She never shares private details. Good searchers stay safe.
